name: Aspata
title: Son of Haman
summary: Aspata belonged to Haman's ten sons and lived in the Persian Empire under King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). His father Haman, called an Agagite, obtained a royal decree that would lead to the destruction of all Jews in the empire. Through Queen Esther's courageous intervention, the plan was exposed and Haman executed. When the appointed day for the attack arrived – the 13th of the month Adar – the Jews defended themselves against their enemies, and Aspata was killed together with his brothers in the fortress of Susa. At Esther's request, the bodies of the ten sons were then hung up as a public testimony that the threat had been averted. The events in the book of Esther, where God's name is not mentioned directly, have in Jewish and Christian tradition been understood as an expression of God's hidden care and guidance of His people amid their exile.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Exaltation and Hatred toward the Jews
keyEvents.description: Aspata's father, Haman, was promoted to the highest position at King Ahasuerus' court, but he developed a deadly hatred for Mordecai and all the Jews.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Plan to Destroy the Jews
keyEvents.description: Haman persuaded King Ahasuerus to issue a decree to destroy all the Jews in the Persian Empire, which threatened the very existence of the entire people.

keyEvents.title: Esther's Intervention and Haman's Downfall
keyEvents.description: Queen Esther revealed Haman's evil plan to the king, leading to Haman being executed on the gallows he had himself built for Mordecai.

keyEvents.title: The Jews' Victory and Aspata's Death
keyEvents.description: When the Jews defended themselves against their enemies on the 13th day of the month of Adar, they killed Aspata and his nine brothers in the fortress of Susa.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Sons Hanged
keyEvents.description: At Queen Esther's request, the king ordered that the bodies of Haman's ten sons, including Aspata, be hung on poles as a public sign that the threat against the Jews had been averted.

versions.summary: Aspata was one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, an enemy of the Jewish people during King Ahasuerus' (Xerxes') reign in Persia. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies on the day Haman's evil plan had set for their destruction. His death marked God's protection of His people during the exile.
versions.title: Son of Haman
versions.reason: [major] Aspata is not described as a 'warrior' in the Bible. There is no information about his role beyond that he was Haman's son. He is mentioned only in the list of Haman's sons who were killed. A more neutral role such as 'son of Haman' or similar would be more precise, but even that is more a family description than a role. The safest approach is to state the role based on what we know.; [minor] The events in the book of Esther are usually dated to the reign of Xerxes I (486–465 BC), that is, the 500s BC, not the 400s. Lifespan should be adjusted to 'c. 500s BC' to better align with the historical timeframe.; [minor] The wording is good, but it can be discussed whether Aspata himself had an active role. The Bible mentions him only as one of Haman's sons who was killed. The expression 'God's protection' is theologically reasonable, but the book of Esther does not mention God explicitly — this is a known feature of the book. A slight nuance may be appropriate.; [minor] Several key events concern Haman and Esther rather than Aspata directly. Although they provide important context, it could be considered whether the descriptions should be linked more clearly to Aspata. Furthermore, it is worth noting that Est 9:7 specifically mentions Aspata's name.; [minor] The wording 'as a public testimony of God's judgment' is a theological interpretation. The text itself only says that Esther asked for them to be hanged, and the king ordered it. God is not mentioned explicitly in the book of Esther.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. Interesting topics to cover include: the meaning of the name Aspata, the Persian/Aramaic background of the names of Haman's sons, the Jewish tradition surrounding the reading of the sons' names in the Scroll of Esther (megillat Ester), and the historical context with the Persian Empire.

He was killed together with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies on the 13th day of the month of Adar, the very day Haman's evil plan had originally designated for the destruction of the Jews. footnotes.text: The name Aspata (Hebrew: אַסְפָּתָא, ʾAspātāʾ) is most likely of Persian origin. Some scholars have attempted to link it to Old Persian words, but the exact etymology remains uncertain. Most of the names of Haman's ten sons appear to have a Persian or Iranian background, reflecting the Persian context in the book of Esther.

In Jewish synagogue tradition, the names of Haman's ten sons (Est 9:7–9) are read in a single breath during the reading of the Scroll of Esther (megillat Ester) on Purim. According to rabbinic tradition, this symbolizes that they all died at the same time and that one should not rejoice excessively over the fall of enemies.

The book of Esther is remarkable because God's name is never explicitly mentioned in the text. Nevertheless, both Jewish and Christian traditions have seen God's providence and hidden hand at work through the events—especially in the dramatic turn where the planned genocide against the Jews was turned into victory.

The events in the book of Esther are historically placed during the reign of Xerxes I (486–465 BC), identified with the biblical Ahasuerus. The Persian capital Susa (Shushan), where the events take place, has been confirmed through archaeological excavations. The excavated palace area corresponds well with the biblical descriptions of the royal court.

In the Hebrew text of Est 9:7–9, the names of Haman's ten sons are written in an unusual vertical column layout, which stands out markedly from the rest of the biblical text. This special presentation has been interpreted in various ways in Jewish tradition, including as a symbol that the sons were hanged on poles.
